newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian opposition sees land rights compromise.
newsitem.headline: Australian opposition sees land rights compromise.

text.p: Australian deputy opposition leader Gareth Evans said on Thursday he remained hopeful of reaching agreement with the government on native title after talks on Wednesday failed to produce a compromise.

"There's a lot of dogged shortsightedness being demonstrated on this by the government, but there is a way through it," Evans told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio. "I've got some residual confidence after last night that we might eventually get there, but it's going to be a long and difficult haul."

Evans and opposition leader Kim Beazley met with Prime Minister John Howard on Wednesday night to discuss the government's 10-point native title plan, which is aimed at ending a bitter land rights row between farmers and Aborigines.

The government hoped to win the Labor opposition's support for the native title legislation to ensure its successful passage through the upper house of parliament, the Senate, where the government does not have a majority.
The opposition said on Monday it believed Howard's native title plan had major discriminatory and constitutional problems.
But Howard has rejected those claims, telling the opposition last night that his plan was not open to negotiation.
"The government's position is that the 10-point plan is the appropriate response to this difficult issue," a spokesman for the prime minister said.
However, Beazley and Howard agreed to hold further talks after the release of the draft legislation, scheduled for later this month.
Howard's plan guarantees farmers' rights to land they have leased since European settlement began more than 200 years ago, while also allowing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.

Native title laws were introduced by the former Labor government three years ago, but became an important political issue when the High Court decided last December that land leased to farmers could be liable to Aboriginal claim.
